prompt: A helper solvent-welds a 3/4-inch potable adapter into a 2-inch PVC sanitary wye so a lavatory faucet can share the chase. What should the journeyman do?

options.text: Cut it out; keep DWV sanitary piping isolated from potable supply
Leave it if the adapter is listed for 140°F drain temperature
Leave it if a dual-check is added on the potable adapter
Leave it only when the fixture is a water-softener brine tank

explanation: Drain, waste, and vent piping is the sanitary drainage system. Codes keep it physically separate from potable water. A faucet supply must not tap a DWV wye; that is a cross-connection and a wrong-system joint, not a chase convenience.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a DWV temperature listing with permission to join potable pipe to a sanitary wye.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a backflow preventer with isolation; a dual-check does not make a potable-to-DWV tap legal.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a licensed plumber with a treatment-plant operator; brine still cannot enter potable piping.

prompt: A 2-inch horizontal kitchen-sink drain is being laid in a crawl space. Under the IPC, what is the minimum slope for that pipe?

options.text: 1/8 inch per foot, the same slope used for 3- to 6-inch drains
1/4 inch per foot, the IPC minimum for 2-1/2 inch and smaller
1/4 inch per foot for 3 inch and smaller; 1/8 inch for 4 inch up
1/2 inch per foot, twice the tabulated value for small drains

explanation: IPC Table 704.1 sets 1/4 inch per foot for horizontal drainage 2-1/2 inch and smaller. A 2-inch sink drain therefore needs 1/4 inch per foot. 1/8 inch per foot starts at 3 to 6 inch; 1/16 inch per foot is for 8 inch and larger.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the 3- to 6-inch slope to a 2-inch drain; small pipe needs 1/4 inch per foot.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses a 3-inch/4-inch split from other codes; IPC drops to 1/8 inch per foot starting at 3 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubles the table; 1/2 inch per foot is steeper than the IPC minimum for a 2-inch drain.

prompt: A first-floor lavatory trap seal is pulled and the water closet gurgles every time an upstairs toilet is flushed. What is the most likely DWV fault?

options.text: The soil stack is being pressurized to speed wastewater flow
The vent is serving as an overflow path during a stoppage
The vent is blocked or missing, so trap seals are siphoned
A missing air gap is letting potable water siphon into the drain

explanation: A vent’s job is to admit air and hold traps at atmospheric pressure. When an upstairs closet discharges into an unvented or blocked stack, negative pressure siphons downstairs seals and causes gurgling. Restore the vent path; do not treat it as a drain or a supply air gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Vents equalize to atmosphere; pressurizing drains blows seals rather than helping flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry vents carry air, not wastewater; using a vent as a relief drain is a code violation.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses DWV venting with potable air-gap protection on the supply side.

prompt: A mop-basin P-trap is being set on a 3-inch floor-sink outlet. What trap-seal depth does the IPC require?

options.text: 1/2 inch min and 1 inch max, as on a shallow drum trap
1 inch minimum, matching the smallest listed trap diameter
1-1/2 inch minimum, matching a common lavatory trap size
2 inch minimum and 4 inch maximum for the water seal

explanation: IPC trap-seal depth is 2 inches minimum and 4 inches maximum, measured from weir to dip. Pipe size (1-1/4, 1-1/2, 3 inch) is not the seal depth. A 1/2-inch or 1-inch seal evaporates or siphons too easily for a sanitary trap.

distractorExplanations.a: A 1/2-inch seal is lost to evaporation or siphonage; code requires 2 to 4 inches.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses trap-seal depth with the smallest trap pipe size; the seal still must be 2 inches.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses 1-1/2-inch trap tubing with seal depth; the water seal is 2 inches minimum.

prompt: A bathroom group uses a 2-inch lavatory-and-tub drain as the vent for the water closet on the same floor. What must remain true of that wet vent?

options.text: The pipe may carry waste and also vent other fixtures within code limits
The pipe may only vent two drains that join at the same elevation
The pipe may also take a roof leader as a sanitary storm vent
An AAV may replace both the wet vent and the building roof stack

explanation: A wet vent is a drain that also vents other fixtures, typically a bathroom group, within size, length, and fixture limits. It is not a dry common vent, not a storm conductor, and it does not let the building drop its required open vent to outdoors.

distractorExplanations.b: Describes a dry common (dual) vent; a wet vent also receives drainage from other fixtures.
distractorExplanations.c: Storm and sanitary must stay separate; a roof leader cannot vent a closet.
distractorExplanations.d: AAVs may supplement island or cabinet vents; they do not erase the wet-vent pipe or the roof terminal.

prompt: A 3-inch building drain turns 90 degrees with two 45s under a slab. Why does the inspector require a cleanout at that change of direction?

options.text: So each fixture trap can be pressure-tested before the slab is poured
So the drain can be rodded at the direction change if it stops up
So the vent stack can be snaked from the roof if frost closes it
So potable shutoffs at the fixture group stay reachable after cover

explanation: Cleanouts give rodding access on the drainage system at changes of direction greater than 45 degrees and at required intervals. Test tees are for the air or water test; vent terminals and supply stops are not DWV cleanout locations.

distractorExplanations.a: Test plugs and testers serve the tightness test; cleanouts exist to rod stoppages.
distractorExplanations.c: Vent terminals are not cleanouts; frost closure is a vent-sizing and termination issue.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses DWV cleanouts with potable shutoff access on the supply side.

prompt: An island kitchen sink cannot take a conventional vent through the cabinet. An AAV is listed and installed on the fixture drain. How does it protect the trap?

options.text: It lets the building omit the required vent through the roof
It dumps sewer gas when the drain develops positive pressure
It admits air on vacuum in the drain, then reseals when idle
It bleeds air from the potable line to stop water-hammer knock

explanation: An air-admittance valve opens only on negative pressure, admitting air so the trap seal is not siphoned, then closes against sewer gas. Codes still require at least one open vent to outdoors for the building drain. AAVs do not relieve positive pressure and are not supply devices.

distractorExplanations.a: AAVs supplement local vents; each building drain still needs a vent to open air.
distractorExplanations.b: AAVs are one-way: they seal on positive pressure and do not dump sewer gas.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an AAV with a water-hammer arrestor on the potable side.

prompt: A 4-inch collector in the basement receives the soil stacks and leaves the foundation wall. What is this piping, and where does it end?

options.text: Building sewer, running from the public main to the property line
Vent header, tying stacks to the roof terminal above the top floor
Fixture branch, taking each trap arm directly into the soil stack
Building drain, taking stacks to the sewer just outside the wall

explanation: The building drain is the lowest horizontal drainage piping that receives stacks and branches inside the structure and conveys them to the building sewer, typically a short distance outside the foundation. The sewer continues to the public main; vents and fixture arms are different parts of the system.

distractorExplanations.a: That run is the building sewer; the building drain is the in-structure collector that feeds it.
distractorExplanations.b: Vent headers carry air to the roof; they do not collect sanitary stacks at the basement.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixture arms and branches serve individual traps; they do not leave the foundation as a 4-inch collector.

prompt: A basement bar sink was roughed with an S-trap: trap, then a vertical drop, and no vent. Why must the journeyman replace it with a P-trap and a vent (or listed AAV)?

options.text: The vertical outlet can siphon the trap seal without a vent
The S-bend traps more debris than a P-trap of the same size
The S-bend makes the seal too deep for the fixture to drain
The S-bend automatically exceeds the maximum trap-arm length

explanation: An S-trap drops vertically immediately after the weir, so discharging water can self-siphon the seal. Codes require a P-trap with a vented trap arm (or a listed AAV where allowed) so air breaks the siphon. Clogging, seal depth, and trap-arm length are separate rules.

distractorExplanations.b: S-traps are banned for self-siphonage, not because they clog more than a P-trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Seal depth is still 2 to 4 inches; the defect is the unvented vertical drop.
distractorExplanations.d: Trap-arm length is a vent-distance rule; the S-trap fails because it siphons its seal.

prompt: A 3-inch horizontal building drain is laid at 1/4 inch per foot. Using typical IPC building-drain tables, about how many drainage fixture units may it carry?

options.text: About 10 dfu, as if it were a 2-inch branch at that slope
About 42 dfu, the usual IPC value for 3-inch at 1/4 in/ft
About 84 dfu, double the 3-inch table, still within 3-inch
About 216 dfu, the IPC 4-inch building-drain value at 1/4 in/ft

explanation: IPC Table 710.1(1) lists about 42 drainage fixture units for a 3-inch building drain at 1/4 inch per foot. Ten dfu is 2-inch territory; 84 dfu overloads 3-inch; 216 dfu is the 4-inch row at the same slope.

distractorExplanations.a: Far too low; a 3-inch drain at 1/4 in/ft is tabulated near 42 dfu, not 10.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubles the table; 84 dfu needs a larger drain, typically 4-inch.
distractorExplanations.d: 216 dfu is the 4-inch building-drain value at 1/4 in/ft, not 3-inch.

prompt: A 3-inch vent stack is being terminated on a two-story dwelling. Where must the open terminal be located?

options.text: In a ventilated attic, a few inches above the insulation
Under a soffit overhang next to the attic intake vents
Open to outdoors, usually through the roof with code clearances
Through a sidewall immediately under an operable bedroom window

explanation: Vent terminals must discharge to open outdoor air, typically through the roof, with the required projection and separation from openings, air intakes, and soffit vents. Ending in an attic, under a soffit, or directly under a window puts sewer gas into the building or back through intakes.

distractorExplanations.a: An attic, even a ventilated one, is still inside the building envelope for sewer gas.
distractorExplanations.b: Codes bar terminals under overhangs with soffit vents because gas is drawn into the attic.
distractorExplanations.d: A terminal may not sit directly under an openable window; IPC needs 10 ft horizontal or 3 ft above.

prompt: A basement floor drain overflows with sewage when the public sewer surcharges after a storm. In DWV terms, what is happening?

options.text: Potable water is back-siphoning from the house into the street main
Fixture trap seals are being pulled by induced siphonage only
Wastewater is flowing normally from fixtures toward the sewer
Wastewater is reversing and discharging back through the fixtures

explanation: In DWV, backflow is reverse flow of wastewater toward and out of fixtures, here from a surcharged public sewer into a basement drain. That is not potable back-siphonage, not trap siphonage from a missing vent, and not ordinary forward drainage.

distractorExplanations.a: That is potable-supply backflow; this event is sewage reversing in the drain.
distractorExplanations.b: Induced siphonage empties traps via vacuum; it does not flood a floor drain with sewage.
distractorExplanations.c: Forward flow goes to the sewer; overflow at the floor drain is reverse flow.

prompt: A restaurant dining room will have an exposed soil stack. Why might the journeyman choose no-hub cast iron instead of PVC for that run?

options.text: Cast iron damps sound; PVC is lighter and solvent-welded
PVC is quieter; cast iron is lighter and joined with solvent
PVC handles higher waste heat; cast iron is limited to dry vents
Cast iron is solvent-welded; PVC is joined with lead and oakum

explanation: No-hub cast iron is heavy, fire-resistant, and much quieter on an exposed stack. PVC is light, noisier, and joined with primer and solvent cement. Cast iron uses no-hub couplings or lead-and-oakum on hub joints and is not limited to vents; it also takes heat better than PVC.

distractorExplanations.b: Swaps the properties: cast iron is heavier and quieter; PVC is the solvent-welded plastic.
distractorExplanations.c: Cast iron tolerates heat better and is used for drains, not only dry vents.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses joining: lead-and-oakum or no-hub for CI; primer and cement for PVC.

prompt: A food-prep room has several floor sinks on one oversized horizontal combination waste-and-vent. Which fixtures may that system serve under typical IPC limits?

options.text: Water closets on a high-rise soil stack with no wet-vent limits
Floor sinks and similar receptors listed for combination waste-and-vent
Potable cold-water mains that also need air relief at the meter
Natural-draft gas appliance vents sharing the sanitary stack

explanation: Combination waste-and-vent is a limited horizontal method for floor drains, floor sinks, sinks, and similar receptors, using oversized pipe in place of individual vents. It is not a high-rise closet stack, not potable piping, and not a fuel-gas vent.

distractorExplanations.a: Water closets are excluded from combination waste-and-vent; they need conventional or wet vents.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses DWV combination venting with potable air relief at a water meter.
distractorExplanations.d: Fuel-gas vents must never share a sanitary stack; that is a combustion-product path.

prompt: Before concealing a new DWV rough-in, the journeyman sets inflatable test plugs in the building drain. What is their purpose?

options.text: Leave them in the cleanouts permanently to block sewer gas
Use them to hydrostatic-test the potable supply before the meter
Isolate the DWV so it can take an air or water test before cover
Cap the roof vent terminal so rain cannot enter the stack

explanation: Test plugs (or test balls) temporarily seal DWV openings so the rough-in can hold an air or water test before concealment. They are removed after the test. Cleanouts get listed plugs, potable piping is tested separately, and vent terminals must remain open in service.

distractorExplanations.a: Test plugs come out after the test; permanent sewer-gas seals are listed cleanout plugs.
distractorExplanations.b: DWV test plugs seal drains; supply lines are capped and tested at working pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: A plugged roof terminal would block venting and siphon traps after occupancy.

prompt: A washing-machine solenoid snaps shut and copper supply in the laundry bangs. What produced the shock?

options.text: Sudden valve closure that launched a pressure surge through the piping
Air trapped in the vent stack after the nearby bathtub drained hard
Slow thermal expansion from the water heater in a closed system
Oversized mains that dropped water velocity well below the design limit

explanation: Water hammer is a supply-side pressure wave from rapid shutoff, typical of solenoid valves and other quick-closing devices. Arrestors or slower closure absorb the surge. Vent air, heater expansion, and oversized pipe are different problems.

distractorExplanations.b: Vent-stack air affects trap seals on the DWV side; hammer is a potable-supply shock from rapid shutoff.
distractorExplanations.c: Thermal expansion raises static pressure slowly and is handled by an expansion tank, not a bang at shutoff.
distractorExplanations.d: Larger pipe lowers velocity and reduces hammer; undersized high-velocity pipe plus quick closure causes it.

prompt: An RPZ or dual-check is set on the domestic water service at the property line. What is it protecting?

options.text: Building drains from sewage backing up out of the public sewer
The potable supply from reverse flow through a cross-connection
The water heater from slow pressure rise due to thermal expansion
Fixture branches from hammer caused by washer solenoid valves

explanation: A backflow preventer on the domestic service stops contaminated water from reversing into the potable main through a cross-connection. Sewer backup, thermal expansion, and water hammer each use different devices.

distractorExplanations.a: Sewer backup into drains is a backwater-valve problem, not a water-service backflow preventer.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed-system expansion is the expansion tank and T&P valve, not the service backflow assembly.
distractorExplanations.d: Hammer arrestors handle pressure surges; the RPZ or dual-check stops reverse contamination.

prompt: A hot-water riser will be Type L or Type M copper at the same nominal size. What is the real difference?

options.text: Type M has the thicker wall; Type L is the thin residential wall
Type L is printed red; Type M is printed blue on the tube
Type L has a thicker wall than Type M; outside diameters match
Type L has a larger outside diameter than Type M at that size

explanation: Drawn copper water tube shares outside diameter by nominal size. Wall thickness runs K (thickest), then L, then M (thinnest), so Type L is heavier than Type M and the inside diameter is slightly smaller. Color marks are L blue and M red.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the order: M is thinner than L; K is the thickest water-tube wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Color codes are swapped: Type L is blue and Type M is red; Type K is green.
distractorExplanations.d: OD is the same for K, L, and M at a given size; only wall thickness and ID change.

prompt: A remodel will replace copper water distribution with PEX. Which claim is a real advantage of PEX?

options.text: UV stability for long exposed runs across a sunlit roof without shielding
Listing for DWV work and solvent-weld joints to PVC drain fittings
Copper-like rigidity, sweat-soldered joints, and wider support spacing
Flexibility, corrosion resistance, and fewer fittings on long runs

explanation: PEX is a flexible pressure-water material that resists scale and corrosion and can snake through framing with fewer fittings. It is not a DWV product, it is not UV-stable outdoors, and it needs closer support than copper.

distractorExplanations.a: PEX degrades in sunlight and must be shielded; UV exposure is a limitation, not an advantage.
distractorExplanations.b: PEX is water-distribution tubing; DWV uses PVC, ABS, or cast iron and cannot be solvent-welded to PEX.
distractorExplanations.c: PEX is flexible, uses crimp or expansion fittings, and needs closer hangers than rigid copper.

prompt: The utility gauge at the meter reads 110 psi static. When must a pressure-reducing valve go on the building supply?

options.text: When street pressure exceeds the typical 80 psi fixture and equipment limit
Whenever an upper-floor lavatory needs a booster because residual pressure is low
On the vent stack so stack pressure cannot siphon nearby fixture traps
Only if the water-heater recovery rate is below calculated fixture demand

explanation: Codes cap static water pressure in the building at about 80 psi. When the street is higher, a listed PRV is installed on the supply after the meter. A PRV does not boost weak pressure, and it does not belong on vents or heaters.

distractorExplanations.b: A PRV lowers incoming pressure; weak upper floors need proper sizing or a booster, not a reducer.
distractorExplanations.c: Vent stacks are DWV; a PRV is a potable-supply device used when street pressure is too high.
distractorExplanations.d: Heater recovery is a BTU/kW rating issue; it does not trigger a building PRV.

prompt: A closed system has a backflow preventer on the service and a storage water heater. What does the expansion tank prevent?

options.text: Hammer bangs when a dishwasher solenoid snaps shut on the hot branch
Excess static pressure as heated water expands with nowhere to go
Scald discharge at showers by blending cold water at the heater outlet
Sediment collecting on the bottom of the tank between annual flushes

explanation: With a check or backflow preventer on the service, heated water cannot push back to the street. Volume growth from heating raises static pressure. A pre-charged expansion tank on the cold inlet absorbs that expansion; it does not stop hammer, scald, or scale.

distractorExplanations.a: Hammer is a shock wave handled by arrestors; an expansion tank absorbs slow volume growth from heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Scald control is a mixing valve or thermostat setting; the expansion tank does not limit outlet temperature.
distractorExplanations.d: Sediment is flushed through the heater drain; the expansion tank does not change scale in the storage tank.

prompt: Copper water tube is joining the steel nipple on a storage water heater. Why install a dielectric union there?

options.text: To bond copper to steel so the piping stays a grounding electrode path
To join PEX to copper without a listed crimp or expansion adapter
To soak up booster-pump vibration at the mechanical-room connection
To isolate dissimilar metals and slow galvanic corrosion at the joint

explanation: A dielectric union electrically separates copper from steel so galvanic current cannot eat the joint in the presence of water. Bonding jumpers restore grounding if required. It is not a PEX adapter and not a vibration isolator.

distractorExplanations.a: The union breaks metal-to-metal continuity; grounding continuity, if required, uses a bonding jumper around it.
distractorExplanations.b: PEX-to-copper transitions use listed adapters; dielectric unions isolate copper from steel or iron.
distractorExplanations.c: Pump vibration uses flexible connectors; the dielectric union's job is corrosion isolation.

prompt: A water-service trench is opening in a frost-prone jurisdiction. What burial rule should the journeyman follow?

options.text: Set the service below the local frost line as the code authority requires
Twelve inches of cover is enough in every cold-climate city on the water service
Match foundation-footing depth even when frost goes deeper than that
Keep the pipe above frost if trench wrap insulation is added on site

explanation: Water service in frost areas is buried below the locally adopted frost line so the line cannot freeze. Cover depth varies by climate and AHJ. Twelve inches is a common sewer-cover figure, not a cold-climate water-service rule, and insulation does not replace frost-line burial.

distractorExplanations.b: Twelve inches is typical minimum cover for some sewers, not frost protection for a water service in cold climates.
distractorExplanations.c: Footing depth may relate to frost but is not the water-service rule; the pipe must sit below the frost line.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrap insulation does not substitute for burial below frost; frozen ground still conducts into a shallow service.

prompt: A hotel shower specification calls for a pressure-balancing or thermostatic mixing valve. What hazard does that valve address?

options.text: Hammer from a guest slamming the shower handle closed on the valve
Scald risk when supply pressure or mixed temperature swings
Reverse flow of shower spray back into the potable riser
Legionella growth inside a remote storage water heater

explanation: Pressure-balancing and thermostatic shower valves keep outlet temperature from spiking when someone flushes a toilet or when hot/cold pressures shift. That is scald protection at the fixture. Hammer, backflow, and Legionella control use other devices and temperature policies.

distractorExplanations.a: Hammer arrestors address surges; mixing valves stabilize outlet temperature, not shock waves.
distractorExplanations.c: Backflow at a shower is a vacuum-breaker or check issue; the mixing valve is a temperature-control device.
distractorExplanations.d: Legionella control stores hot water hot; the shower mixer prevents scald at the outlet, not biofilm in the heater.

prompt: On a new domestic service, where is the utility water meter typically set?

options.text: On the water-heater outlet so only hot use is billed by the utility
Downstream of the building PRV so the meter sees reduced street pressure
At the service entrance so all incoming water to the property is measured
On every fixture branch so the utility can bill each fixture separately

explanation: The utility meter sits at the service connection so every gallon entering the property is measured. Building PRVs, heaters, and fixture branches are downstream of that meter. Submeters, if used, are owner devices, not the typical utility location.

distractorExplanations.a: Some owners submeter hot water, but the utility meter is on the incoming service, not the heater outlet.
distractorExplanations.b: The meter is at the service; a PRV is installed after the meter so it does not starve or under-read the account.
distractorExplanations.d: Utility billing uses one service meter; per-fixture meters are not the standard service location.

prompt: A three-story apartment has long developed length from the heater to distant baths. What does a hot-water recirculation pump do?

options.text: Raise the heater recovery rate so the tank reheats faster after a draw
Boost cold-water residual pressure at the farthest lavatory on the riser
Blend cold into the hot loop in place of a thermostatic mixing valve
Keep hot water moving in the loop so fixtures deliver heat sooner

explanation: A recirc pump circulates already-heated water through a return loop so the branch is hot when a fixture opens. It does not add heater input, does not boost cold mains, and is not a scald-mixing valve. Codes often require recirc or heat trace when developed length is long.

distractorExplanations.a: Recovery depends on burner or element input; the pump only moves water already in the tank and loop.
distractorExplanations.b: Recirc serves the hot loop to cut wait time; it does not raise cold-supply residual pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Anti-scald mixing is a separate valve; the recirc pump's job is delivery time, not temperature limit.

prompt: Sweating a copper potable-water joint. Which procedure produces a sound, code-legal connection?

options.text: Clean and flux the cup, heat the fitting, and let solder wick into the joint
Melt solder in the torch flame onto a cold, dirty, unfluxed fitting cup
Brush flux on after the copper is already glowing so the flux will not burn
Use 50/50 tin-lead solder because it wets copper better than lead-free alloys

explanation: A capillary solder joint needs clean metal, flux applied before heat, and heat on the fitting so solder melts on the copper and is drawn into the cup. Potable lines require lead-free solder. Flame-melted solder on a cold joint and post-heat flux both fail.

distractorExplanations.b: Solder must melt on the heated, fluxed metal and wick in; dropping molten solder on cold copper will not bond.
distractorExplanations.c: Flux goes on cleaned surfaces before heating; applying it after heat defeats cleaning and wetting.
distractorExplanations.d: Lead-bearing 50/50 solder has been banned on potable water; use listed lead-free solder.

prompt: A cation-exchange softener is piped on the cold supply ahead of a storage heater. What does the resin actually do?

options.text: Add calcium carbonate to raise pH of acidic well water
Swap hardness ions (calcium and magnesium) for sodium or potassium
Dose chlorine from the brine tank to disinfect the building supply
Strip taste and odor the way a granular activated-carbon bed does

explanation: Softener resin exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium or potassium, which is what 'softening' means. Regeneration uses brine. Calcite beds raise pH, chlorine disinfects, and carbon treats taste and odor—those are different treatments.

distractorExplanations.a: Calcite neutralizers add calcium to raise pH; softeners remove calcium and magnesium, they do not add them.
distractorExplanations.c: The brine tank holds salt to regenerate resin; a softener is not a chlorinator.
distractorExplanations.d: Carbon filters adsorb taste, odor, and chlorine; ion exchange swaps hardness ions, not organics.

prompt: A journeyman is sizing the cold-water riser for a multi-bath dwelling. Which load method matches water-supply tables?

options.text: Add drainage fixture units from the DWV tables and pick the next steel size
Run every branch at 2 inch so velocity and pressure loss never matter on the riser
Convert fixtures to water-supply fixture units and size from the code charts
Match the street-main diameter regardless of fixture count in the building

explanation: Water distribution is sized from water-supply fixture units (WSFU) and the adopted Hunter-style charts, then checked for available pressure and velocity. Drainage fixture units size DWV, not the cold riser. Oversizing every branch or copying the street main ignores actual demand.

distractorExplanations.a: DFUs size drains and stacks; water piping uses WSFU because flow coincidence on supply is a different curve.
distractorExplanations.b: Blind 2-inch branches waste material, drop velocity control, and still may starve distant fixtures if pressure is low.
distractorExplanations.d: Street-main size is not the building load; a small house on a large main still sizes from WSFU and pressure.

prompt: Hotel showerheads are being replaced on a renovation. What is the federal maximum flow for a showerhead?

options.text: 1.6 gallons per minute measured at 60 psi
3.5 gallons per minute measured at 80 psi
4.0 gallons per minute measured at 100 psi
2.5 gallons per minute measured at 80 psi

explanation: The Energy Policy Act cap for showerheads is 2.5 gpm at 80 psi. Some WaterSense or local rules go lower, but 2.5 gpm at 80 psi is the federal ceiling. 1.6 gpm is a toilet flush figure; 3.5 gpm is the old pre-1992 shower rate.

distractorExplanations.a: 1.6 gallons is the federal toilet flush volume, not the showerhead flow cap of 2.5 gpm at 80 psi.
distractorExplanations.b: 3.5 gpm was common on older showerheads; EPAct 1992 cut the federal limit to 2.5 gpm at 80 psi.
distractorExplanations.c: 4.0 gpm at 100 psi is well above the federal showerhead limit of 2.5 gpm at 80 psi.

prompt: A floor-mount water closet is specified with a standard 12-inch rough-in. From which points is that 12 inches measured?

options.text: From the open stud face to the front lip of the closet flange
From the wood framing to the back edge of the closet flange
From the finished wall surface to the center of the closet flange
From the finished wall surface to the flange center, using 15 inches

explanation: The common residential closet rough-in is 12 inches from the finished wall (not the studs) to the center of the closet flange. Measuring to a flange edge or from open framing shifts the bowl into the wall or leaves a gap. Fifteen inches is a side-clearance figure, not the rear rough-in.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses stud-face-to-flange-lip with finished-wall-to-flange-center; drywall thickness would then put the bowl too close to the wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Using the back edge of the flange and the framing, not the flange center and finished wall, misplaces the closet bolts.
distractorExplanations.d: Fifteen inches is the usual minimum from a water-closet centerline to a side wall, not the rear-wall rough-in.

prompt: A powder-room lavatory is being finished. What supply-stop and trap arrangement matches typical IPC/UPC fixture rules?

options.text: Accessible stops on the supplies and an S-trap set to the listed trap-arm height
Concealed in-wall stops and a drum trap under the lavatory bowl
One shutoff at the water heater and a crown-vented trap at the lavatory
Accessible fixture stops on the supplies and a vented P-trap at proper height

explanation: Each lavatory needs accessible fixture stops so the faucet can be serviced without shutting the house, plus a vented P-trap set to the code trap-arm height. S-traps, drum traps, and crown vents are prohibited because they siphon or are not serviceable fixture traps.

distractorExplanations.a: S-traps are prohibited in new work; they self-siphon. A lavatory needs a vented P-trap, not an S-trap even if the height looks listed.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops must remain accessible; concealing them in the wall and using a drum trap both violate typical fixture rules.
distractorExplanations.c: A heater shutoff is not a fixture stop, and a vent at the trap weir (crown vent) is prohibited.

prompt: A dishwasher drain hose is tied into a kitchen sink with a disposer. What connection protects the hose from waste backing up?

options.text: A high loop or listed air gap, then into the disposer or sink drain above the trap
A hose tap into the tailpiece on the sewer side of the trap weir
A check valve on the dishwasher hot-water supply inlet and no drain air gap or loop
A vacuum breaker threaded onto the drain hose at the disposer inlet

explanation: Codes and listings require an air gap or a high loop under the counter so sink waste cannot siphon back into the dishwasher. The hose then joins the disposer nipple or a wye on the sink drain above the trap. Supply check valves and vacuum breakers do not replace that drain air break.

distractorExplanations.b: Tapping downstream of the trap bypasses the seal and admits sewer gas; the hose must join above the trap with a loop or air gap.
distractorExplanations.c: A supply check valve does not protect the drain hose from dirty sink water; the drain still needs a high loop or air gap.
distractorExplanations.d: Vacuum breakers protect potable supply outlets; dishwasher drain hoses use an air gap or high loop instead.

prompt: A mechanical-room floor drain will see water only a few times a year. Why does the spec call for a trap primer?

options.text: It vents the floor-drain trap so siphonage cannot pull the water seal dry
It meters small amounts of water into the trap so evaporation does not break the seal
It acts as a backwater flap that blocks sewer backup onto the floor
It timed-flushes debris out of the trap on a programmed wash cycle

explanation: Seldom-used floor drains lose trap seal by evaporation. A trap primer (or a listed equivalent) adds makeup water so the seal stays full. Venting fights siphonage, a backwater valve fights backup, and primers are not debris-flush machines.

distractorExplanations.a: A primer adds water to offset evaporation; the vent addresses siphonage, a different way of losing the seal.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a backwater valve. A primer feeds small makeup-water doses and does not stop sewer surcharge.
distractorExplanations.d: Primers deliver tiny makeup amounts; they are not designed to scour debris from the trap on a timer.

prompt: A mortar-bed tile shower is being built over a liner. When must the receptor be proven watertight?

options.text: Cement backer board may serve as the waterproof layer under the tile
A topical sealer coat over finished tile is accepted as the shower pan
The liner or membrane must be waterproof and flood-tested before tile is set
Flood-test the receptor after grout has cured so leaks show at the tile face

explanation: The shower pan or bonded membrane is the waterproof layer. It is installed and flood-tested before mortar and tile so leaks can be repaired without demolition. Cement board is not a pan, and a sealer over grout is not a code receptor.

distractorExplanations.a: Cement board is a substrate, not a waterproof pan; a liner or membrane must still be installed and tested.
distractorExplanations.b: The pan sits under the mortar bed; a topical sealer on finished tile is not the listed shower receptor.
distractorExplanations.d: Testing after grout means tearing out finished tile to find a liner leak; the flood test is done on the bare pan.

prompt: A food-waste disposer is added under a kitchen sink. What else must the installation provide?

options.text: A dedicated vent stack separate from the sink trap and vent
A hot-water supply branch piped into the disposer to soften grease and food waste
A trapless drain tied straight into the building drain
A listed electrical connection and a drain that still uses the sink trap and vent

explanation: A disposer is both an appliance and a fixture outlet: it needs a listed electrical hookup and it discharges through the sink’s trap and vent. It does not get its own stack, a water-supply tap, or a trapless run to the building drain.

distractorExplanations.a: The disposer uses the sink trap and vent; a separate dedicated stack is not required for a standard kitchen disposer.
distractorExplanations.b: Disposers have no water-supply connection; makers tell users to run cold water so fats solidify and flush.
distractorExplanations.c: Every fixture drain needs a trap; a disposer cannot bypass the sink trap into the building drain.

prompt: An electric bidet seat is added to an existing water closet. What does a typical listing plus bathroom electrical rules expect?

options.text: A protected potable supply, often hot and cold, and a nearby GFCI receptacle
Its own 3-inch trap and a dedicated vent stack hidden in the plumbing chase
A tee off the closet fill valve with no vacuum breaker or air gap
A hardwired 240-volt circuit that skips GFCI in the bathroom

explanation: Washlets and bidets need a backflow-protected water supply (many use hot and cold) and, for electric seats, a 120-volt GFCI receptacle in the bathroom. They do not need a 3-inch trap and stack, an unprotected tee on the closet fill, or a 240-volt non-GFCI circuit.

distractorExplanations.b: A bidet fixture uses a small 1-1/4 inch trap on ordinary venting; an add-on seat uses the closet trap, not a new 3-inch stack.
distractorExplanations.c: A spray outlet on potable water needs an air gap or vacuum breaker; an unprotected tee off the closet fill is a cross-connection.
distractorExplanations.d: Electric bidet seats plug into a 120-volt bathroom receptacle that needs GFCI protection, not a 240-volt hardwired circuit.

prompt: A commercial restroom will have wall-hung water closets off a chase. What is the carrier system there for?

options.text: Floor-mount closets bolted through a cast-iron closet bend
A concealed frame that supports wall-hung closets, urinals, or lavatories
Horizontal drain piping hung on straps from the floor joists
A water-heater stand that lifts the storage tank a few inches off the floor

explanation: A fixture carrier is a rated steel frame in the wall or chase that takes the load of a wall-hung closet, urinal, or lavatory and ties the fixture to the drain. Floor-mount closet flanges, pipe hangers, and heater stands are different supports.

distractorExplanations.a: Floor-mount toilets bolt to a closet flange; carriers hold wall-hung fixtures off the floor from inside the chase.
distractorExplanations.c: Pipe hangers support horizontal drains; a carrier is the fixture frame, not a DWV hanger.
distractorExplanations.d: Heater platforms are not carriers; carriers anchor wall-hung lavatories, urinals, and water closets.

prompt: After trim is on a pressure-balancing tub/shower valve, the plumber sets the temperature limit stop. What does that stop do?

options.text: It forces a minimum hot rotation so mixed water stays above 120°F
It restricts shower flow to 2.5 gpm in place of the showerhead flow restrictor
It limits how far the handle can turn toward hot so outlet temperature is capped
It resets the water-heater thermostat for every fixture in the house

explanation: The limit stop is a mechanical rotation stop on the valve cartridge. It caps how far the handle can go toward full hot so shower outlet temperature stays at the scald-protection setting (often 120°F max). It does not set a minimum temperature, a flow rate, or the heater thermostat.

distractorExplanations.a: Limit stops cap maximum hot rotation to prevent scalding; they do not force mixed water to stay above 120°F.
distractorExplanations.b: Flow is limited by the showerhead; the limit stop only restricts handle travel toward hot.
distractorExplanations.d: The heater thermostat sets storage temperature for the system; a limit stop caps outlet temperature at that one valve.

prompt: A wall-mount lavatory faucet is specified. What must be in the wall before finishes close?

options.text: Adhesive drywall anchors without wood or steel blocking behind the valve
Rough-in postponed until after tile so the spout height can still be moved
A deck-mount valve body set in the lavatory’s back ledge instead of the wall
Correct valve rough-in dimensions and solid blocking behind the faucet

explanation: Wall-mount faucets hang on the valve body. The rough-in depth and height must match the trim, and solid blocking must carry the load. Drywall anchors, waiting until after tile, or swapping in a deck-mount body will leak or pull out.

distractorExplanations.a: Drywall cannot carry faucet loads; wall-mount valves need solid blocking and the listed rough-in.
distractorExplanations.b: Wall-mount rough-in is set before tile and close-in; spout height cannot be adjusted after finishes.
distractorExplanations.c: A deck-mount body is a different faucet type; wall-mount trim needs an in-wall valve with backing.

prompt: A wall-hung urinal is specified with a flushometer, not a tank. How is that fixture flushed?

options.text: Line-pressure water through a flush valve scours the fixture
A gravity tank that refills through a float valve after each flush
A waterless cartridge that seals with a barrier liquid and uses no flush water
Building compressed air piped to the rim to scour the urinal bowl

explanation: A flushometer uses building water pressure through a flush valve (manual or sensor) to rinse the urinal. Gravity tanks, waterless cartridges, and compressed-air scouring are other fixture types, not flushometer urinals.

distractorExplanations.b: Gravity tanks are typical of residential water closets; flushometers use line pressure through a flush valve.
distractorExplanations.c: Waterless urinals use a cartridge and no flush water; a flushometer urinal delivers a pressurized water flush.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressure-assist closets use air in a vessel; flushometer urinals rely on supply-water pressure, not shop air.

prompt: A laundry closet needs a washing-machine outlet box in the wall. What does that box provide?

options.text: A trapped floor drain with a primer directly under the washer
A recess for hot and cold stops and the standpipe drain opening
A surface-mounted air-gap fitting as the washer’s discharge path
A dryer-vent collar with a backdraft damper in the same plastic box

explanation: A washing-machine box recesses the hot and cold fixture stops and the standpipe (or drain opening) so the hoses and discharge sit in the wall cavity. A floor pan, a standalone air-gap fitting, and a dryer vent are separate items.

distractorExplanations.a: A floor pan or drain is extra protection; the washer box itself houses the valves and the standpipe opening.
distractorExplanations.c: Washers discharge into a standpipe with an air break at the box; the box is not merely a surface air-gap fitting.
distractorExplanations.d: Dryer-vent boxes are a different product; the washing-machine box is for water valves and the drain.

prompt: An accessible public lavatory is being set. Which combination matches ADA rules the plumber has to coordinate?

options.text: A pedestal lavatory with the rim at 36 inches, which also gives the required knee and toe space
Twist-knob faucet handles and a rim height of 38 inches above the finished floor
Knee clearance under the bowl, a rim no higher than 34 inches, and lever or sensor controls
Exposed hot supplies and an uninsulated P-trap left bare so knees can reach the piping

explanation: ADA lavatories need knee and toe clearance, a rim no higher than 34 inches, and controls that work without tight grasping or twisting (levers or sensors). Pedestals block knees, 36–38 inch rims are too high, and hot pipes under the bowl must be insulated or shielded.

distractorExplanations.a: ADA caps lavatory rim height at 34 inches and requires knee clearance, which a pedestal base blocks.
distractorExplanations.b: Twist knobs fail the operable-parts rule, and 38 inches exceeds the 34-inch rim maximum.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot water and drain pipes under accessible lavatories must be insulated or wrapped to protect knees; leaving them bare is the injury trap.

prompt: A frost-proof wall hydrant (sillcock) is run through an exterior wall in a freeze climate. How does it keep from bursting?

options.text: A heat-trace cable on the outdoor barrel keeps the hydrant valve body from freezing
An antifreeze reservoir inside the hydrant body protects the seat
Water is left pressurized in the outdoor barrel so ice cannot form
The valve seat sits inside the heated space so the outdoor barrel drains when shut

explanation: A frost-free sillcock uses a long stem so the valve seat is in the heated wall cavity. When the handle is closed, the outdoor barrel drains (a hose must be disconnected). Heat tape, antifreeze pots, and a pressurized outdoor barrel are not how listed frost-proof hydrants work.

distractorExplanations.a: Frost-free sillcocks do not rely on heat trace; the long stem places the seat inside the heated space.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no antifreeze charge; the seat is indoors and the barrel drains when the valve is shut.
distractorExplanations.c: Pressurized water left in the outdoor barrel would freeze and split the hydrant; the design drains that barrel.

prompt: DWV and water are stubbed for fixtures with the walls still open. When is the fixture rough-in inspection done?

options.text: After all fixtures are set, to verify flow and drainage at the final visit
While piping is still exposed, before walls close, to check layout, slope, and joints
After drywall is hung but before tile, to check pipe supports that are already covered
Before any underground piping is laid, as a trench-depth check with no pipe in the ground

explanation: Fixture rough-in inspection happens while the piping is still open in the walls and floors so the inspector can see layout, grade, supports, tests, and connections. Final inspection is after fixtures are set. Underground inspection is a separate earlier step on buried pipe.

distractorExplanations.a: That is the final inspection after trim; rough-in is done before concealment while joints are visible.
distractorExplanations.c: Once drywall is up the piping is concealed; rough-in cannot verify slope and joints behind board.
distractorExplanations.d: Underground inspection is on installed buried pipe; it is not the above-grade fixture rough-in, and it is not a trench with no pipe.

prompt: A journeyman is bidding a four-story apartment in a city that adopted the International Plumbing Code. Unless the ordinance amends it, which model code governs the plumbing?

options.text: The ICC International Plumbing Code as adopted by the city
The IAPMO Uniform Plumbing Code even though the city listed IPC
NFPA 54 fuel-gas rules used as the whole plumbing code
ASME A112 fixture standards standing in for the plumbing code

explanation: Jurisdictions adopt a model plumbing code by ordinance. Where the city adopted the IPC, that ICC document—plus any local amendments—is the enforceable plumbing code. The UPC is a different IAPMO model code and is not in force unless the city adopted it instead.

distractorExplanations.b: IAPMO's Uniform Plumbing Code is a separate model; it does not override a city's IPC adoption.
distractorExplanations.c: NFPA 54 covers fuel gas, not the full plumbing system of fixtures, DWV, and water supply.
distractorExplanations.d: ASME A112 standards list fixtures and fittings; they are not a substitute for the adopted plumbing code.

prompt: Permit drawings for a medical office cite the Uniform Plumbing Code throughout the spec. Which organization publishes that model code?

options.text: ICC, the publisher of the International Plumbing Code (IPC)
NFPA, the publisher of NFPA 54 fuel gas and fire codes
IAPMO, which writes and publishes the Uniform Plumbing Code
ASME, through A112 fixture and fitting product standards series

explanation: The Uniform Plumbing Code is IAPMO's model plumbing code. ICC publishes the IPC, NFPA publishes fire and fuel-gas documents, and ASME writes product standards such as A112—none of those bodies publish the UPC.

distractorExplanations.a: ICC publishes the IPC, a competing model code, not the Uniform Plumbing Code.
distractorExplanations.b: NFPA publishes NFPA 54, NFPA 13, and related fire/fuel-gas codes, not the UPC.
distractorExplanations.d: ASME A112 addresses fixtures and fittings; ASME does not publish the UPC model code.

prompt: A listed vacuum breaker is on the truck, but the inspector says it cannot be used on this hose bibb. Who has final approval authority in that jurisdiction?

options.text: The model-code publisher that wrote the adopted code text
The general contractor managing the overall construction project
The listing laboratory that certified the plumbing product
The local official or office that enforces the adopted code

explanation: The Authority Having Jurisdiction is the local official or office that adopts, interprets, and enforces the plumbing code and issues permits. Listing and model-code text inform that decision, but they do not replace the AHJ's approval power.

distractorExplanations.a: ICC and IAPMO write model codes but have no local enforcement or permit power.
distractorExplanations.b: The contractor must comply; the contractor is not the enforcing authority.
distractorExplanations.c: Listing labs certify products to a standard; the AHJ still decides job-site approval.

prompt: A homeowner asks the journeyman to skip the permit on a water-heater change-out to finish before a weekend. Why must the permit still be obtained?

options.text: So the AHJ can inspect the work for public health and safety
So the city assumes all liability if the work later fails
So the manufacturer warranty on the heater can be registered
So the assessor can revalue the house for property taxes

explanation: Plumbing permits exist so the AHJ can review and inspect work that affects public health and safety—gas, combustion air, T&P relief, and potable connections. Skipping the permit hides those checks; it does not transfer liability or create a warranty.

distractorExplanations.b: A permit does not shift defect liability onto the city; it triggers code inspections.
distractorExplanations.c: Warranties are registered with the manufacturer, not created by the plumbing permit.
distractorExplanations.d: Assessors may see permit data, but the code purpose is health-and-safety inspection.

prompt: The water utility requires a reduced-pressure backflow assembly on a fire-sprinkler tap from the domestic main. What is the cross-connection program meant to prevent?

options.text: Sewer gas entering occupied rooms through dry fixture traps
Keep contaminated water from entering the potable supply
Keep storm inflow from entering the building sanitary sewer
Water-hammer surges on the municipal distribution main

explanation: Cross-connection control stops backflow of nonpotable or contaminated water into the potable system. Fire lines, irrigation, and boilers are typical hazards; approved backflow assemblies and testing programs protect the public water supply.

distractorExplanations.a: Sewer gas is controlled by traps and vents, not by backflow assemblies on the water main.
distractorExplanations.c: Storm inflow is an I&I or storm-drain issue, not a potable-water cross-connection program.
distractorExplanations.d: Surge control is hydraulic; cross-connection programs address contamination, not hammer.

prompt: A supplier offers unmarked pipe that 'the last crew ran for years' on a potable riser. When is a material approved under the plumbing code?

options.text: When the manufacturer labels the box as plumbing-grade stock
When the contractor has used the same unmarked product on prior jobs
When it is listed for that use to a code-referenced standard
When one listing for DWV automatically covers potable pressure

explanation: Code-approved materials are those listed or accepted for the intended use to a referenced standard and accepted by the AHJ. A maker's marketing label or prior-job habit is not approval, and a DWV listing does not authorize potable pressure service.

distractorExplanations.a: A manufacturer's own 'plumbing-grade' sticker is not a listing to a referenced standard.
distractorExplanations.b: Field familiarity is not code approval; unmarked pipe cannot be accepted on that basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Listings are use-specific; DWV-rated pipe is not automatically approved for potable pressure.

prompt: A single bathroom group—water closet, lavatory, and tub—needs a new vent. Unless the local table is stricter, what size does the vent typically start at?

options.text: 1/2 inch, matching a typical lavatory or ice-maker supply
3/4 inch, matching a common water-heater T&P relief line
1 inch nominal, matching many fixture cold-supply risers
1-1/2 inches, the usual start for a bathroom-group vent

explanation: Model codes set a minimum vent of 1-1/4 inch, and a bathroom group that includes a water closet is commonly vented at 1-1/2 inch (or larger per the local DFU table). Half-inch through 1-inch sizes are supply tubing, not DWV vents.

distractorExplanations.a: 1/2 inch is a water-supply size; it is far below the code minimum vent diameter.
distractorExplanations.b: 3/4 inch is a relief or supply size and is below the 1-1/4 inch vent minimum.
distractorExplanations.c: 1 inch still undersizes the vent; bathroom-group vents typically start at 1-1/2 inch.

prompt: Remote lavatories starve when several fixtures run at once, even though the meter looks large. How does the plumbing code size water piping?

options.text: Fixture units, developed length, and remaining pressure
Drainage fixture units plus the slope of the building drain
A velocity cap only, ignoring friction over developed length
Meter size alone, matched to the building main shutoff valve

explanation: Water-supply sizing uses water-supply fixture units, developed length, and available pressure (minus friction and elevation). Velocity limits are a check, not the whole method. Drainage fixture units and slope size the DWV system, not the supply.

distractorExplanations.b: DFUs and slope size drains and vents; they do not size potable supply piping.
distractorExplanations.c: Velocity matters, but friction over developed length and remaining pressure also control size.
distractorExplanations.d: The meter is one constraint; branches are still sized from fixture units, length, and pressure.

prompt: A client wants shower and laundry waste stored and pumped to landscape irrigation. Where gray water is allowed, what must the system do?

options.text: Tie into the potable supply through a single check valve
Remain separated, filtered, and limited to approved uses
Hold untreated gray water in the tank for at least 72 hours
Include kitchen-sink waste and toilet discharge in the same tank

explanation: Where permitted, gray-water systems must stay physically separated from potable piping, meet filtration/disinfection and storage limits, and serve only approved uses such as subsurface irrigation. Kitchen waste and soil waste are blackwater, not gray water.

distractorExplanations.a: A single check valve is not backflow protection; gray water must not interconnect with potable piping.
distractorExplanations.c: Codes typically cap untreated storage (often about 24 hours) to limit odor and bacterial growth.
distractorExplanations.d: Toilet discharge is blackwater; many codes also exclude kitchen sinks from gray-water collection.

prompt: An apprentice cannot tell how a waste stack turns from a floor plan alone. What does an isometric plumbing drawing show that a plan view does not?

options.text: A scaled plan view of piping as seen from directly above
A single-wall elevation of fixture heights on one face
A 3D-style view of pipe runs used to read the routing
A building cross-section showing structural member loads

explanation: Isometric plumbing drawings show piping in a 3D-style view, typically with 30-degree offsets, so vertical stacks and horizontal runs can be read on one sheet. Plan and elevation views are 2D; structural sections are not plumbing isometrics.

distractorExplanations.a: A plan is a top-down 2D view; an isometric is drawn to show three-dimensional routing.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevations show one wall face; they do not replace a system-wide isometric.
distractorExplanations.d: Structural sections show building loads; they are not used to lay out plumbing isometrics.

prompt: During a restaurant remodel, both a plumbing inspector and a health inspector walk the kitchen. What may the health department specifically regulate?

options.text: Branch circuit wiring for water heaters, pumps, and disposers
Structural notching and boring limits at plumbing holes
The utility's rate schedule for municipal water service
Plumbing sanitation in food sites and public health facilities

explanation: Health departments commonly overlay extra sanitary rules on food-service and public-health plumbing—indirect wastes, mop sinks, grease control, and hand-wash fixtures. Electrical, structural, and utility-rate issues belong to other agencies.

distractorExplanations.a: Electrical inspectors enforce wiring to equipment; health departments do not adopt the electrical code.
distractorExplanations.b: Notching and boring limits are building-code structural rules, not health-department plumbing.
distractorExplanations.c: Water rates are a utility or commission matter, not a health-department plumbing regulation.

prompt: A reduced-pressure principle assembly on a boiler fill is specified as ASSE 1013. What do ASSE standards typically cover?

options.text: Backflow preventers and related plumbing-device performance
Fitting dimensions in the ASME B16 product-standards series
The model plumbing code text adopted by states and cities
Fire-sprinkler installation rules under NFPA 13 standards

explanation: ASSE (now IAPMO/ASSE) writes performance standards for plumbing devices—backflow preventers, mixing valves, and similar products. Model codes come from ICC or IAPMO; B16 is ASME; sprinkler installation is NFPA 13.

distractorExplanations.b: ASME B16 covers fitting dimensions; it is not an ASSE plumbing-device performance standard.
distractorExplanations.c: IPC and UPC are model codes; ASSE publishes device standards, not the adopted code text.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 13 governs sprinkler installation; ASSE 1013 is a backflow-preventer performance standard.

prompt: The adopted IPC table shows a 12-inch bury, but the city ordinance requires water service 42 inches deep. What may local code amendments legally do?

options.text: Apply to a single permit instead of the whole jurisdiction
Modify the model code for local climate or soil conditions
Take effect from an inspector's verbal preference alone
Replace the adopted code with manufacturer instructions

explanation: Governing bodies adopt the model code by ordinance and may amend it for local conditions such as frost depth, seismic rules, or water quality. Amendments apply jurisdiction-wide; a verbal inspector preference or a one-job deal is not an amendment.

distractorExplanations.a: A one-job change is a variance or modification, not a code amendment.
distractorExplanations.c: Amendments must be formally adopted; an inspector's preference is not code.
distractorExplanations.d: Manufacturer instructions apply through listings; they do not replace the adopted code.

prompt: A new DWV stack is plugged and ready for the inspector. What is the common model-code tightness test for drainage and vent piping?

options.text: A 5-foot water head or 3 psi air held 15 minutes with no loss
A 10-foot water head or 5 psi air held 5 minutes with no loss
A 10-foot water head or 5 psi air held 15 minutes with no loss
A 100 psi water or 50 psi air test held 15 minutes with no loss

explanation: IPC/UPC DWV testing commonly requires a 10-foot water column or a 5 psi air test held 15 minutes with no pressure or water-level loss. Water-supply tests use much higher pressures and must not be applied to DWV piping.

distractorExplanations.a: A 5-foot head or 3 psi air is below the usual 10-foot / 5 psi DWV test.
distractorExplanations.b: The pressure values match, but the hold time is 15 minutes, not 5.
distractorExplanations.d: Those pressures belong to water-distribution tests; they can damage DWV joints.

prompt: A helper wants to sit the journeyman exam after two weeks of carrying pipe. What does a typical journeyman plumber license require?

options.text: Completing a short online quiz with no documented field hours
Skipping apprenticeship, related instruction, and field hours
Showing a deed or lease in the licensing city or county
Completing documented experience and passing the trade exam

explanation: Most jurisdictions require documented apprenticeship or equivalent hours plus a trade exam before issuing a journeyman plumber license. A two-week helper stint, an online quiz, or property ownership does not meet those experience and testing requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Licensing boards require documented hours and a proctored trade exam, not a short online quiz.
distractorExplanations.b: Apprenticeship or equivalent supervised experience is the usual path, not a waiver of all training.
distractorExplanations.c: Homeownership is unrelated to trade competence or licensing eligibility.
